The first: If it is correct that his name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, how does Allah mention him by a name that carries the meaning of shirk?

The second: Many people became known by their kunyas, and their names were not known. Ibn Qutayba said: "One who is not alone reported to me, from al-Asma'i, that Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu Sufyan ibn al-'Ala' — their names were their kunyas. So if the name of Abu Lahab was his kunya, then He mentioned him only by that by which he is known."

[p. 260]

His saying ﴿What his wealth availed him﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited his nearest kin to Allah, Abu Lahab said, 'If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself with my wealth and my children.' So Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿What his wealth availed him, nor what he earned﴾."

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Ma* (ما) is in the nominative position. The meaning: what his wealth and his earnings availed him, i.e., his child." Likewise, the commentators said that what is meant by *kasb* (earnings) here is his child. *Aghna* (أغنى) has the meaning of *yughni* (يُغْنِي).

﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾, meaning it will blaze upon him without smoke. ﴿And his wife﴾, meaning his wife will also burn. She is Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan.

In this is evidence for the truth of the prophethood of our Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, for he informed of this matter: that he and his wife would die upon disbelief, and so it was. For if they had said with their tongues, "We have embraced Islam," the disbelievers would have found a pretext to reject the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). But Allah knew that they would not embrace Islam, neither inwardly nor outwardly, so He informed him of that.

﴿The carrier of firewood﴾: On this there are four opinions.

The first: She used to walk about spreading slander. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and al-Farra'. Ibn Qutayba said: "They likened slander to firewood and enmity and rancour to fire, because these arise through slander, just as fire blazes up from firewood."

The second: She used to gather thorns and throw them on the path of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at night. This was narrated by 'Atiyya from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said likewise.

The third: What is meant by the firewood is sins. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: She used to reproach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for his poverty, and she used to gather firewood, so she was reproached for that. This was said by Qatada. But it is not strong, because Allah described him as possessing wealth.

'Asim alone read *ḥammālata* (حَمّالَةَ) *al-ḥaṭab* (الحَطَبِ) with the accusative (*naṣb*).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever reads *ḥammālata* in the accusative does so in dispraise, meaning: 'I mean the carrier of firewood.'" *Al-jid* (الجِيدُ) means the neck.

*Al-masad* (المَسَدُ) in the language of the Arabs is a rope when it is made of the fibre of the *muql* palm. It may also be said of ropes made of camel hair. The poet said:

*And a twisted rope of red, aged she-camels, with marrow that is full-bodied.*

Ibn Qutayba said: "Many people think that *masad* refers only to palm fibre, but this is not so. *Masad* is anything that is twisted and braided, whether of fibre or of other materials."

The commentators differed about what is meant by this rope, and there are three opinions.

The first: They were ropes that existed in Makkah. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak said: "It is a rope of tree bark with which she gathered firewood."

The second: It is a necklace of palm fibre (*min wada'*). This was said by Qatada.

The third: It is an iron chain seventy cubits (*dhira'*) in length. This was said by 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr. Others said: What is meant by this rope is the chain that Allah mentioned in the Fire, whose length is seventy cubits. The meaning is that this chain has been twisted tightly, and she is tormented with it in the Fire around her neck.
